note: Voice-over per scene. Each line is tied to a visual beat with Narration.cue(i) in the scene file (scenes/common.py). Thread: broken agents -> patterns -> we built a game factory -> what the factory makes -> what frontier models do on its games -> why the score is trustworthy -> the games as training data -> why it matters. Lines marked OPEN in SCRIPT.md are left out until the 07:00 lock.

lines: Break one AI agent, and you learn one thing: it broke.
Look closer. This model walks into the same wall eleven times, sure it is one step from the goal.
This one wanders into a dead end, and resets far too late.
Now break thousands of them, on games none of them has ever seen.
The pieces stop being noise. They line up into patterns.
Each pattern is something agents still can't do. To find them at scale, we built a game factory.
The factory writes games from code. Every new seed is a new game, so the supply never runs out.
Each game shows the agent only this: sixty-four by sixty-four pixels, sixteen colours. No text, no score, no rule names.
It has six buttons. That's all.
Colours and shapes are reshuffled in every game, so nothing can be memorised.
Each new level hides one new rule, which the agent must discover by experimenting.
And a search proves every level solvable, so we always know the best possible run.
We ran frontier models on fresh games, first with our own harness.
Then the way labs benchmark them: the full conversation, and maximum reasoning effort.
None of them matches the optimal run.
Where does the gap come from? We log every move, with what the model believed. This one is sure that moving right reaches the goal. The screen never changes.
This one stays stuck for a long time before it tries a reset.
This one acts on a belief the screen has already disproved.
Each failure gets a label. And everything they needed was on the screen.
To trust these numbers, the score has to be hard to game. It rewards solving levels efficiently, and nothing else.
On the judges' own harness, doing nothing scores zero, and stopping after one level earns only that level.
Resetting never erases the moves already spent.
And the score is computed in a separate container that the agent cannot reach.
Because the supply never runs out, the games are also training data. Can a small model learn from them?
We compare it against a control trained on the same amount of non-game data, so any gain comes from the games, not just from more training.
That makes the factory useful beyond this hackathon: private evaluations that can't leak, and endless training environments for labs.
Every broken agent shows where AI still has to learn.
Game Factory. Try to beat the AI yourself.
